title: Writing It Down So Others Can Build It
segs: Chapter 7. Writing It Down So Others Can Build It.

When the founders approved the project, Imran Qureshi drew the guard on a napkin from the sweet shop below the office. The drawing took four minutes. A long box on the left was labelled "message", and a long box on the right "safe message". Between them stood four small boxes in a row, each with three words beneath it.
A napkin sketch is a guess about structure. You can't build from it. It doesn't say what each box must do, how anyone will know the box works, or what happens when it fails.
In this chapter we follow the sketch as it becomes a document that a stranger could build from. Then we see the first test of the design, done on paper.
The case: four boxes on a napkin.

Imran's sketch split the work into four parts. Anaya had three jobs. She had to say exactly what each part was responsible for. She had to write the conditions under which each would count as finished. And before any code existed, she had to find out whether the people who would use the result could understand it.
What the guard is made of.

The sketch gives each kind of personal detail to the part best suited to find it. The table lists the four parts, and why each one is separate. Read the third column carefully, because it is the reasoning behind the design.

Table 7.1: The four parts of the guard. Pattern checker. What it does: Finds details that always have the same shape: a PAN (five capital letters, four digits, one capital letter), an Aadhaar number (twelve digits), a mobile number (ten digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9) Why it is separate: A fixed rule finds these instantly, at no cost, the same way every time. Name-and-place finder. What it does: Finds details with no fixed shape, such as a person's name, an address or an employer. Why it is separate: No rule can describe "Ramesh Jain" or "14 Sector 15, Gurgaon"; something must read the sentence and recognise a person or a place. Context judge. What it does: Reads the few sentences the first two parts could not settle and decides whether they point to a person. Why it is separate: Reading in context is slow and costly, so it is asked only about what remains. Rule-keeper. What it does: Decides what to do with each detail that was found. Why it is separate: It finds nothing itself; it applies the rules for each kind of detail.
The pattern checker is the first part. The name-and-place finder is the second.

The context judge is the third part. To see why it is needed, think of a quasi-identifier. That's a detail that is harmless alone but can point to one person when combined with others. Here is an example: "I am the only diabetic patient in my village who had a transplant last year". The sentence has no number and no name, and it still identifies someone.
The rule-keeper is the fourth part. For each detail it chooses among four actions.

It can redact the detail. That removes it completely and leaves a label such as [PAN] in its place. It can mask it. That hides part of the detail but keeps its shape, so a mobile number becomes 98 … 12 and the agent can see that a number was there. It can let the detail through. Or it can ask a person.
The choice depends on why the information was collected. A delivery address is needed for a delivery. An identity number isn't needed to ask about late fees.
Starting from the problem.

A PRD, or product requirements document, says what to build and why. The "why" matters. Engineers make better decisions when they know the problem, and worse ones when they get a list of features with no purpose attached.

Anaya began where a PRD should begin, with the problem and its evidence: the 37 conversations, the interview numbers, and the greeting that invited details. Next came who the tool was for, and who it was not for. Then came scope, including a section on what was left out on purpose. She filled that one from the Won't list in the strategy.

After that she described what the user would see in four situations: when the tool worked, when it was unsure, when it failed, and when it declined. The remaining sections covered the tests the tool had to pass, how success would be measured, how it would be released, and what was not yet known.
The test of the whole document was a single question. Could a stranger build this and know when they had finished? The answer depended almost entirely on one section.
Done, in a way that can be checked.

The part of a PRD that does the most work is the set of conditions for "done". These are the acceptance criteria, and each one should be something you can test. The most common failure is a criterion that can't be tested.
The table pairs some weak criteria with the same ones rewritten.

Table 7.2: Acceptance criteria that cannot be tested, and the same ones rewritten. It finds identity numbers accurately. Can be tested: At least 95 of every 100 identity numbers in a set of real conversations, marked by hand beforehand, are hidden. It is fast. Can be tested: It adds no more than a third of a second to a reply. It handles bad input. Can be tested: If a message is empty or only emoji, it passes through unchanged and nothing is logged as an error.
Notice that the first rewritten criterion doesn't say every number will be found, because that wouldn't be true. It says how many, out of what, measured against what.

For a tool that reads and writes text, "done" isn't a promise of one correct answer. It's a rate, measured on examples that someone has already marked, with a limit written down. The marked examples are what give the rate its meaning. Anaya didn't have them yet, so she put that on the open-questions list in capitals.
Stories and odd cases.

Each piece of work needs a short description from the user's side, with its own conditions. A user story describes one piece of value. For example: as a support agent, I want identity numbers hidden as I read the chat, so that I never see what I don't need.

A variant, the job story, starts from the situation instead of the role. It gives engineers more to work with. For example: when I open a chat for a customer asking about a loan, I want any identity number hidden, so that I can help without handling it.
After the stories come edge cases. These are the unusual inputs that the ordinary cases never touch, and most of the real work hides in them. Farah's team and Imran's memory supplied a list.

Table 7.3: Edge cases for the guard. A number written with spaces or dashes: 4321-5678-9012. What should happen: Hide it as if it were written normally. A number broken over two lines. What should happen: Hide both halves. "adhar" or "mobil" misspelled beside a number. What should happen: Still hide the number. A mobile number already half hidden: 98xxxxxx12. What should happen: Leave it alone and do not report it. A twelve-digit order number that is not an identity number. What should happen: Do not hide it, or the agent cannot do the job. A message in Hindi script with Hindi digits. What should happen: Hide it. The tool cannot decide. What should happen: Say so and let a person decide.
Anaya added the last row herself, and it separates a product from a gamble. Software that reads text will sometimes be unsure. A product has to say in advance what it does then.
The thinnest thing that works.

Imran proposed to build the guard in layers. First would come the part that reads the chat, then the finding, then the hiding, then what the agent sees. By the sixth week everything would work together.
Anaya asked what would work in the fifth week. "Nothing," he said.

That's the problem with cutting work in layers. Nothing is usable until the last layer is done. If you cut it in slices instead, you build a thin version of every layer, and something works from the start. A vertical slice passes through all the layers, narrowly.

Anaya specified the first one. It handled a single kind of number, written in a single way. It followed that number from the moment a message arrived to the moment an agent saw it hidden, with a line in a log saying what was done.
Definition: Minimum viable product.
An MVP is the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption with real users. It isn't a small version of everything. It's one small version of the one thing that has to be true.
Two weeks at a time.

Imran's team worked in sprints, which are fixed periods of two weeks. Each sprint begins with a plan. It ends with a demonstration and a short meeting about what went well and what should change. The demonstration shows working software, never slides.
Estimates were harder. Imran could say how long a rule for twelve digits would take. He couldn't say how long it would take to find names in Hinglish, because he didn't know whether it could be done.

So the team used a time-box. That's a fixed amount of time, with a decision at the end of it. Here it was three days. If fewer than seventy of every hundred names in the real conversations were found by then, they would stop and rethink. A time-box turns a guess about duration into a decision point.
Paper first.
Anaya drew the agent's screen on four sheets of paper.
The chat with a number masked. The same chat with a note saying "1 detail hidden, click to see why". A chat where the tool was unsure. A chat where it had hidden something the agent needed.

A rough, cheap version made to learn something is called a prototype. How much care it deserves depends on the question you're asking. Paper can show whether a flow makes sense. A clickable mock-up can show whether people find their way. A version that runs on real output can show whether they trust it.

On Friday she sat down Neha, a colleague of Farah's, at a table with the four sheets. She didn't give instructions. She set a task: a customer says her callback number was hidden, so find out what happened.
This is a usability test. It's simple to describe and hard to carry out, because its whole discipline is not helping.

Neha picked up the second sheet and looked at it for eleven seconds. She picked up the third, put it down, and asked where she should click to get the number back. Anaya wanted very much to point, and kept still. "There is no way to get it back," Neha said to herself. "So I'd have to ask Imran."
Key idea: What eleven seconds found.

A test with three to five people like Neha reveals most of the serious problems in a design, and each hesitation is a finding. Anaya added a line to the PRD: an agent can see the hidden detail, for one chat, with a reason recorded. No meeting had raised it.
Chapter summary.

A specification starts from the problem, says what is left out, and states "done" as conditions that can be tested. For anything that reads and writes text, "done" is a rate measured against examples someone has already marked.

The guard has four parts: a pattern checker for fixed shapes, a name-and-place finder for details without shape, a context judge for what remains, and a rule-keeper that decides what to do. Each detail is redacted, masked, passed or queried. Stories describe value from the user's side, and edge cases are where most of the real work hides. A product must say what it does when it is unsure. The first version is a vertical slice that goes through every layer narrowly, and an MVP tests the riskiest assumption. Sprints keep the team in step with working software, and a time-box ends uncertain work with a decision. A paper prototype, tested on a real person who isn't helped, finds problems that a meeting would not.
That finishes the planning. Next, Anaya and Imran begin to look at the machine itself.
